questions.question: A linear constraint $\sum_j a_{ij}x_j\le b_i$ has a negative right-hand side $b_i<0$. What does the negative right-hand-side transformation do with it?
options: Multiply all coefficients and $b_i$ by $-1$, and turn $\le$ into $\ge$.
Multiply only $b_i$ by $-1$ and keep the direction $\le$ unchanged.
Multiply every coefficient and $b_i$ by $-1$ and keep $\le$ unchanged.
Move $b_i$ to the left-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes 0.

questions.question: An equality constraint $\sum_j a_{ij}x_j=b_i$ has $b_i<0$ and is multiplied by $-1$ to obtain a nonnegative right-hand side. Which relation does the result have?
options: It becomes a $\ge$ constraint, since multiplying by $-1$ reverses.
It becomes a $\le$ constraint, since the sides are interchanged.
It stays an equality, since $u=v$ holds exactly when $-u=-v$ does.
It becomes a pair of strict inequalities, one in each direction.

questions.question: Why does the elementary simplex starting construction apply the negative right-hand-side transformation to constraints with $b_i<0$?
options: Because a negative $b_i$ makes the linear program infeasible.
Because the transformation enlarges the set of feasible decisions.
Because simplex can only handle constraints of the form $\le$.
Because that start is built from nonnegative right-hand sides.

questions.question: A linear program contains $x_1-x_2\le-1$, which is replaced by $-x_1+x_2\ge1$. How does this affect the set of feasible decisions $(x_1,x_2)$?
options: It grows, as the right-hand side is larger.
It stays exactly the same set of decisions.
It shrinks, since $\ge$ is a stricter direction.
It is mirrored, since the coefficient signs change.

questions.question: A linear program with objective $\max\, 3x_1+2x_2$ contains a constraint with a negative right-hand side, which is multiplied by $-1$. What happens to the optimal solution?
options: It moves, since one of the constraints has changed its direction.
It keeps its point, but the optimal value changes sign.
It changes unless the objective is also multiplied by $-1$.
It stays the same: feasible set and objective do not change.

questions.question: Apply the negative right-hand-side transformation to the constraint $3x_1-2x_2\le-6$. Which constraint results?
Multiply the equality $-x_1+4x_2-x_3=-5$ by $-1$ so that its right-hand side becomes nonnegative. What is the resulting constraint?
A constraint reads $2x_1-x_2\ge-4$. After the negative right-hand-side transformation, which constraint results and what is its direction?
options: $2x_1-x_2\le4$, now a $\le$ constraint
$-2x_1+x_2\ge4$, still a $\ge$ constraint
$-2x_1+x_2\le4$, now a $\le$ constraint
$2x_1-x_2\ge4$, still a $\ge$ constraint

questions.question: In a production model with $x_1,x_2$ the amounts of two products, a constraint is written as $-x_1-x_2\le-10$. What does it require once the negative right-hand side is removed?
options: $x_1+x_2\le10$: at most 10 units in total
$x_1+x_2=10$: exactly 10 units in total
$-x_1-x_2\ge10$: no production at all
$x_1+x_2\ge10$: a total of at least 10

questions.question: A constraint $x_1-3x_2\le-2$ is transformed into $-x_1+3x_2\ge2$. Which added variable turns this new constraint into an equation?
options: A surplus variable, subtracted from the left-hand side.
A slack variable, added to the left-hand side.
No variable, since the right-hand side is now positive.
A slack variable, subtracted from the right-hand side.

questions.question: A linear program contains $x_1-2x_2\le0$. Must the negative right-hand-side transformation be applied to it?
options: Yes, since the coefficient of $x_2$ is negative.
Yes, since only positive right-hand sides are allowed.
No, since a right-hand side of 0 is already nonnegative.
No, but only because the constraint is of the $\le$ type.

questions.question: Why must the inequality sign reverse when a constraint $\sum_j a_{ij}x_j\le b_i$ is multiplied by $-1$?
options: Because the simplex method only accepts constraints of type $\ge$.
Because multiplying both sides of $u\le v$ by $-1$ gives $-u\ge-v$.
Because a positive right-hand side always comes with a $\ge$ sign.
Because reversing the sign keeps the origin among the feasible points.

questions.question: Instead of multiplying $x_1-x_2\le-1$ by $-1$, a student multiplies it by $-2$ and writes $-2x_1+2x_2\ge2$. Is this an acceptable replacement?
options: No, since only multiplication by $-1$ keeps the same feasible set.
Yes, but it doubles the region of feasible decisions $(x_1,x_2)$.
No, since the right-hand side must equal the old one in absolute value.
Yes, since any negative factor with reversal keeps the feasible set.

questions.question: The constraint $3x_1-5x_2\le-2$ is transformed into $-3x_1+5x_2\ge2$. Consider the point $(x_1,x_2)=(2,1)$. Which forms of the constraint does it satisfy?
options: Neither form, since $3\cdot2-5\cdot1=1>-2$
Both forms, since $3\cdot2-5\cdot1=1\ge-2$
Only the original form, since $3\cdot2-5\cdot1=1\le2$
Only the transformed form, whose right-hand side is positive

questions.question: A linear program has the constraints (a) $x_1+x_2\le4$, (b) $x_1-x_2\ge-2$, (c) $-x_1+2x_2=-3$ and (d) $2x_1-x_2\le0$. Which of them should the negative right-hand-side transformation be applied to?
options: (b) and (d)
(c) only
(b) and (c)
(b), (c) and (d)

questions.question: A student rewrites $-x_1+x_2\le-3$ as $-x_1+x_2\le3$, changing only the sign of the right-hand side. Which point shows that this changes the problem?

A modeller turns $x_1-x_2\le-1$ (with $x_1,x_2\ge0$) into an equation by adding a variable $s\ge0$: $x_1-x_2+s=-1$, without first transforming it. Why can this not give a starting solution with $x_1=x_2=0$?
options: An equation with a negative right-hand side cannot be solved.
Setting $x_1=x_2=0$ gives $s=1$, which overstates the allowance.
An added variable may only be used in $\ge$ constraints.
Setting $x_1=x_2=0$ forces $s=-1$, which violates $s\ge0$.

questions.question: After the transformation, $x_1-x_2\le-1$ becomes $-x_1+x_2\ge1$, which has a positive right-hand side. Does the transformation make the point $x_1=x_2=0$ feasible?
options: No; the feasible set is unchanged, and the origin violates both of the forms.
Yes, since multiplying by $-1$ moves the origin into the feasible region.
Yes, since every constraint with a nonnegative right-hand side holds at the origin.
No, but the origin was feasible for the original form before the change.

questions.question: A linear program with $x_1,x_2\ge0$ contains $-3x_1+2x_2\ge-12$. It is transformed, and then a variable $s\ge0$ is added to the left-hand side to obtain an equation. What value does $s$ take when $x_1=x_2=0$?
options: $s=-12$, so no valid start
$s=12$, so the start is allowed
$s=12$, but a surplus is needed instead
$s=-12$, unless an extra variable is added

questions.question: For $x_1,x_2\ge0$, a student transforms $3x_1-x_2\le-3$ into $-3x_1-x_2\ge3$, forgetting to change the sign of $-x_2$. What does this error do to the model?
options: Nothing serious, as $(0,3)$ satisfies both versions
It only cuts off the points whose $x_2$ is larger than 3
It leaves no feasible point, though $(0,3)$ was feasible
It enlarges the region, since $3$ exceeds $-3$
